[[RunningHead]]

Concerning the Nature of Psychoanalysis: The Persistence of a Paradoxical Discourse. Gregorio Kohon. New York: Routledge, 2019. 140 pp.

Adam Pollock

Adam Pollock

Adam Pollock  

In his recent book, Concerning the Nature of Psychoanalysis: The Persistence of a Paradoxical Discourse (2019), the Argentine-born, adoptively British author and psychoanalyst Gregorio Kohon writes, “The real strength of Freudian psychoanalysis continues to reside in its insistence and tenacity, in its commitment to the remarkable persistence of its paradoxical discourse” (p. 2). It's easy to grant that psychoanalysis is a discourse—what isn't, these days?—but how is it paradoxical? Kohon doesn't say outright, but the answer seems bound up with his task of defending and defining psychoanalysis against the prescriptive, evidence-based, and overly simplified preferences of the health-industrial complex. In its defensive action, the book is something of a polemic. This can be heartening; but it's Kohon's attempt to define psychoanalytic discourse in itself that I find most engaging.

Maybe the paradoxical nature of the psychoanalytic discourse has to do with the seeming conflict embedded in a practice that seeks to communicate the experience of the analytic encounter, as expressed through the medium of the single case study. “Such study does not seek to formulate laws nor generalise results that are necessarily applicable to other subjects; whatever the hypothesis and/or conclusions, there is neither assumption nor certainty that they would correspond to other cases” (p. 7). Yet, when we learn to practice psychoanalysis, we necessarily do so by reference to the “exemplars” (Kohon uses Thomas Kuhn's term) described by such study. “People wanting to train in psychoanalysis will be expected to know the psychoanalytic exemplars, from Freud's original clinical cases onwards. And there is, of course, no fixed set, no limited numbers of exemplars” (p. 10). If, at the macro end, the set of exemplars can't be encompassed, the micro end is scarcely more manageable. “If that weren't slippery enough, it's all subjective, too: “two observers witnessing the same phenomenon may be steeped in two radically different theories and thus will see two different things” (p. 8).

Esther Swim-Wright   Graduate degrees from Michigan State University and the University of North Carolina and is currently studying modern psychoanalytic group therapy at the Center for Group Studies in New York City. She is a board member of and coordinates workshops for the Carolinas Group Psychotherapy Society. She worked as a clinical social worker in the North Carolina state psychiatric system and is currently in private practice in Durham, providing adult individual and group psychotherapy.

An individual's experience of a modern psychoanalytic process group, attended virtually during the COVID-19 pandemic, is explored by the author using a metaphor of underground fungus networks, mycelia, as a signifier to examine the experience. Instances of acting out that are unique to the digital therapy experience illustrate the tension between doing and the mandate to put everything into language while “in” the room.

In 2015, colleagues from the British Psychoanalytic Society began meeting to discuss contemporary politics for a series called The Political Mind Seminars. The group presented papers interpreting various subjects, including democracy, Brexit, neoliberalism, climate change, and the Trump presidency. In his introduction to The Unconscious in Social and Political Life, a 2019 essay collection that presents the first ten of these seminars, editor David Morgan states, “I am aware that many analysts do not consider the political world a suitable place for psychoanalysis to venture” (p. xxxiv). But these gatherings continued to cover prevailing issues and only became more and more popular. The series is ongoing.

Morgan says that it was the magnitude of the 9/11 attack on America that spurred him to look at unconscious process in political thought, inspiring the seminars and this book (p. xiii). In Clinical Implications of the Psychoanalyst's Life experience: When the Personal Becomes Professional, Kuchuck (2014) writes that “September 11th, 2001, was the first time that my patients and I were experiencing trauma and retraumatization at the same time” (p. xxii). [[RunningHead]]

White privilege: Psychoanalytic perspectives. Neil Altman. New York: Routledge, 2021. 94 pp.

William Sharp

William Sharp

William Sharp  

White Privilege: Psychoanalytic Perspectives (Altman, 2021) is a volume in the Psychoanalysis in a New Key book series. “When music is played in a new key, the melody does not change, but the notes in the composition do” (p. iv), writes the series editor, Donnel Stern. Like a well-trained musician, Altman modulates white privilege into a psychoanalytic key.

This short book is steeped in object relations and relational theory. The preface and introduction are a must read to appreciate the frame and structure of Altman's assertion. In the preface, Altman writes, “The full integration of good and bad in the depressive position requires a refusal to leave behind splitting altogether.” (p. x). The subsections of the introduction begin to outline terms necessary to join the conversation on white privilege, including Lynne Layton's “normative unconscious” (p. 5), which is defined as the way we learn how the world works early in life. Since this becomes part of our character so early, it is preverbal, therefore requiring a lot of curiosity and patience to understand. The chapters are titled with the very terms they define: whiteness, privilege, guilt, power, liberalism, and conservatism. The last part of the book addresses how these concepts can play out in the consulting room: “What psychoanalysis has to do with it” and how to move “Toward a more perfect union.” In my experience, my own evolving awareness of white privilege follows a parallel process to the layout of the book as we move from introduction, to defining very nuanced terms, to then beginning to see why and how we can begin to address them in the consulting room.

Altman speaks to the need for psychoanalytic professionals to begin to think about key terms that need to be understood if we hope to promote psychoanalysis as a body of knowledge. Altman made a smart choice to spend more time outside the consulting room, as that seems to be his ongoing challenge and imperative for the viability of contemporary psychoanalysis.

A comprehensive clinical portrait is drawn of a 13-year analysis of “Linda,” utilizing Kohut's notion of “the grandiose self” as a framework for understanding the case. The theory of dreams has changed fundamentally since Freud's time, when their primary function was seen as protecting sleep by distorting and hiding repressed material from consciousness. Many contemporary psychoanalysts emphasize the transformative function of dreams, to create sense and meaning for lived experience. Consequently, the way we use dreams in our daily clinical work has changed radically. The dream is no longer viewed as belonging exclusively to the analysand. We listen to virtually any verbal and nonverbal communication as a joint dream of the analytic couple, dreamed in the here-and-now. The author discusses this paradigm shift in light of analytic field theory and the phenomena of hallucinosis, dreaming, and reverie (both visual and somatic). Clinical examples are provided to illustrate the theory and the application of this approach.

Sensitivity, Isolation, and Loneliness in the Treatment of Schizoid Personality Disorder

John Madonna

John Madonna

Email: Drjmadonna@verizon.net

John Madonna   Licensed psychologist, training analyst, faculty member, supervisor and teacher at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis. He has written and presented papers on the treatment of children, adolescents and adults. He is coauthor of two books: The Play Therapy Treatment of Sexually Abused Children and Treating Police Stress, and is the editor of Emotional Presence in Psychoanalysis: Theory and Clinical Applications

This paper examines seminal psychoanalytic theory regarding the etiology of schizoid personality disorder and discusses considerations for treatment. In light of prevalent theory and citing case material, essential features of the analyst's calibrated emotional presence in the treatment of those suffering from this affliction, as well as the promotion of a curative sense of ordinariness, are discussed. In line with this, particular attention is paid to the challenges, resistances and suffering experienced by both patient and analyst as they attempt to relate. Primary among these challenges is the debilitating sensitivity, isolation, and loneliness of the schizoid person, which complicates the desire to relate, confining the person to the shadows of interpersonal life.

Introduction

William Hurst

William Hurst

William Hurst  

This issue of Modern Psychoanalysis contains several talks delivered at the CMPS 2021 conference on “Dreaming the Session,” all focusing on the topic through the lens of psychoanalytic field theory. Lawrence Brown discusses what can occur spontaneously in the immediacy of a session with the psychotherapist, and what symbols can form and connect in that space; Barbara D'Amato takes a look at those symbols deep within a dream-scape of the artistic matter we consume; and Civaterese, the conference's keynote speaker, explores the space between and around: How the dream is no longer perceived as solely a creation of the analysand: the dream as merely one encapsulating many, a joint dream of the analytic couple, in the moment to moment of time, and in the space of a field.

Civitarese has regarded “Merleau-Ponty as a precursor of the analytic field”. He writes that few psychoanalysts cite the writings of Merleau-Ponty due to an apparent lack of familiarity with his work, not knowing, therefore, the significance and utility his thought could have for psychoanalysis (Civitarese 2015, 151-169). He co-edited, with Howard Levine, Growth and Turbulence in the Container/Contained: Bion's Continuing Legacy, and with Gabriela Legorreta, On Freud's “Formulations on the Two Principles of Mental Functioning” He has written extensively on various topics, including the Oedipus complex, trauma, countertransference dreams, the analytic setting, aspects of Bion's work, autistic spectrum disorders in children, and psychoanalytic field theory.

The author examines and discusses the three named modes of experiencing and processing the analytic relationship, focusing on the responses of the analyst to the patients' functioning and relating to the analyst and to the process. He considers those responses not only as developed therapeutic techniques but also, and especially, as spontaneous, naturally generated and emotionally informed and charged elements of the relationship.

Don't Wake Me Up

Barbara D'Amato PsyaD LP

Barbara D'Amato

Email: drbarbaradamato@gmail.com

Barbara D'Amato   Faculties of the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies (CMPS) and the New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis (NYGSP). She is director of the CMPS Distance Learning Program. She has had an interest in dreams and dreaming for many years and has written extensively on literary authors and their dreams, the function of aggression in dreams, and the modern psychoanalytic approach to working with dreams. She has presented internationally on dream topics and research. Her forthcoming paper, “A Waking Dream: Condensation and Symbolism in Bob Dylan's ‘Murder Most Foul’,” addresses the Bionian topic of continuous dream states as well as Freud's most important dream formulations. She is in private practice in Brooklyn and Manhattan.

The author reflects on dreams, prompted by and responding to Dr. Civitarese's and Dr. Brown's presentations, as communications both internally (between the dreamer and her own unconscious) and, when reported in session, with the analyst. In tandem with this the author explores dreams as expressions of otherwise inacccessible interior perceptions and preoccupations.

Poetry and Psychoanalysis: The Opening of the Field. David Shaddock. London and New York: Routledge, 2020, 176 pp.

Nancy Gerber

Nancy Gerber

Nancy Gerber  

If poetry is the spontaneous overflow of emotion recollected in tranquility, as Wordsworth declared, perhaps psychoanalysis is the expression and acceptance of unconscious longings and wishes in the transference. Poetry and psychoanalysis share an intense engagement with language, symbolic meaning, silences, and other nonverbal communicative elements such as rhythm and tone.

David Shaddock, a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and a published poet, explores these and other resonances between the two fields of endeavor in his new book, Poetry and Psychoanalysis: The Opening of the Field. The “field” of the subtitle also refers to the intersubjective field of the analytic encounter, as discussed in this issue of the journal, a relational space charged with meaning akin to Winnicott's “transitional space”—the area between inner and outer reality—and Beebe's realm of the infant/mother dyad (p. xvii, p. 4). Shaddock frequently returns to the theme of a gap, a separation between self and Other that can be bridged through empathic listening and shared perception. He cites Kohut as one of his psychoanalytic heroes, and there are many references to Kohut's theory of transference, his break with Freudian drive theory, and his emphasis on empathy.

[[RunningHead]]

“I Am Not There. I Did Not Die.”

On a Future Psychodynamic Treatment Paradigm for Combat Trauma, Moral Injury and War Psychoses

Amir Kohen MA

Amir Kohen

Email: akohenpsych@gmail.com

Amir Kohen   New York Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, and has done some training in the advanced clinical program at the Institute for Psychoanalytic Training and Research (an IPA institute in New York). He is currently a co-chair in military communications for the APA Division 19: Society for Military Psychology. He is based in Tel Aviv, Israel, and is currently training at IDC Herzliya, Lauder School of Government in homeland security and counterterrorism.

The author interrogates two propositions: one, in developing a conceptual framework for the relationship between psychosis and trauma, is there something importantly distinct about “combat trauma” or “combat psychosis” that differentiates it from other similarly presenting psychopathology? The other, is there a treatment paradigm by which we can structure combat psychosis within psychoanalytic and psychodynamic discourse and theory? This is brought into conversation with experiences of acute psychosis, trauma, and suicidality in post-9/11 US combat soldiers living in a psychiatric residence for veterans in New York City, from February 2019 to March 2020. Clinical observations are then related to ontology utilizing Camus's “absurd/l'absurde.”

The Analyst's Desire: The Ethical Foundation of Clinical Practice. Mitchell Wilson. New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2020. 234 pp.

Paul Moore

Paul Moore

Paul Moore  

The analyst's desire is a term borrowed from Lacan but used by Wilson as he attempts to integrate the concept with related ones used in other schools of thought. It applies in his use of it here to the role of the psychoanalyst's desire in creating the space for an analysis to occur. This space has an ethical component, because it grants access to the discourse of the Other (the unconscious, as referred to by Lacan). When a space that allows access to the Other is maintained, an additional opening occurs where the desire that is unique to the patient can emerge and be seen by the analyst. Thus, ethical considerations here deal with maintaining an analytic space and what may happen when an analyst's own desire has not been adequately processed, and how subjective reactions to a patient can often be related to the role of the analyst's desire within treatment. There is a slight difficulty in the discussion, here, in that “the analyst's desire” is conceived of differently from time to time. Sometimes it's Lacan's particular conceptualization, and sometimes it can refer more generally to the analyst's subjective reactions, which may be more closely related to what is traditionally understood as subjective countertransference.
